query: Consider the following context: The recent trend of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) was studied extensively for their promising mechanical properties, but individual constituents' effects have remained unexplored. In that context, which method can be used for the effects of changing the percentage of elements of HfNbTaTiZr-HEA on the mechanical properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: In the HfNbTaTiZr high‐entropy alloy, increasing the concentration of Hf while systematically adjusting the percentages of the other elements (via a DOE-guided combinatorial approach) will enhance yield strength due to increased solid solution strengthening and lattice distortion, while possibly diminishing ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr-HEA produced by established synthesis techniques (e.g., spark plasma sintering) displaying baseline mechanical properties.
generation.intervention: Employ a Design of Experiments (DOE) approach paired with high‐throughput synthesis to systematically vary the individual elemental percentages, specifically increasing Hf content relative to the other elements.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing performed under standardized quasi-static loading conditions at room temperature with all samples undergoing identical processing and heat treatment protocols.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced local lattice distortion and solid solution strengthening due to increased atomic size mismatch from higher Hf content.
generation.mechanism: A higher concentration of Hf increases local lattice distortions, which impedes dislocation motion, thereby raising the yield strength. This same increased lattice distortion may also lead to reduced plasticity and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the equiatomic baseline, samples with increased Hf content will exhibit a directional increase in yield strength accompanied by a measurable decrease in ductility, although the precise quantitative effects remain uncertain.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr-HEA synthesized and tested under identical conventional conditions.
generation.boundary: The predicted effects are expected within the limited compositional variations studied (e.g., adjustments of +/- 10% for individual elements) and under standard processing and testing conditions; interactions among multiple elements outside this range may alter the response.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the mechanical property changes is uncertain due to complex multi-element interactions and potential processing variations; only directional trends (increased strength and reduced ductility) are anticipated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HfNbTaTiZr-HEA samples with systematically varied compositions by increasing the Hf content (while adjusting the other elements to maintain overall balance) using a factorial DOE approach. Process all samples under identical conditions and perform standardized mechanical tests.
measurements: Yield strength (via tensile or compressive testing)
Ductility (measured as the total strain at failure)
Microstructural analysis (using SEM/TEM to quantify lattice distortions)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with increased Hf content do not show a directional increase in yield strength and a corresponding decrease in ductility compared to the equiatomic baseline, or if the microstructural analysis does not reveal increased lattice distortion, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High entropy alloys (HEA) have been one of the most attractive groups of materials for researchers in the last several years. Since HEAs are potential candidates for many (e.g., refractory, cryogenic, medical) applications, their properties are studied intensively. The most frequent method of HEA synthesis is arc or induction melting. Powder metallurgy is a perspective technique of alloy synthesis and therefore in this work the possibilities of synthesis of HfNbTaTiZr HEA from powders were studied. Blended elemental powders were sintered, hot isostatically pressed, and subsequently swaged using a special technique of swaging where the sample is enveloped by a titanium alloy. This method does not result in a full density alloy due to cracking during swaging. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed powders resulted in a fully dense but brittle specimen. The most promising result was obtained by SPS treatment of gas atomized powder with low oxygen content. The microstructure of HfNbTaTiZr specimen prepared this way can be refined by high pressure torsion deformation resulting in a high hardness of 410 HV10 and very fine microstructure with grain size well below 5

The requirements for designing novel metallic alloys that are capable of surpassing a whole set of specific properties of currently available commercial alloys are, at present, a subject of high demand in the industry. For instance, an improved combination of metallic alloys should possess strength and ductility while maintaining a relatively low cost. This is especially true when one is dealing with materials for high-temperature applications. Therefore, new engineering solutions are needed for novel materials that outperform the capabilities of the currently used Ni-based alloys. One of the prospective innovative materials that could be able to meet the requirements of such demanding applications, especially in the aviation and aerospace industries, may be refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs). These are also known by other names, such as complex concentrated alloys (CCAs). These materials have been extensively studied in recent years [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ] due to their very interesting combination of properties in some of the compositions.
